fr:mainmatter.html:p: Part of Modern Web Browser from Within Emacs. Supersedes the text-rendering half of Tree Rendering in Emacs by aiming instead for full HTML-quality rendering inside an Emacs buffer.

Goal: when previewing a tree in Emacs, show a rendering that matches what the Forester-compiled HTML shows in a real browser — rendered math, transclusions expanded inline, working links, Datalog query results, figure images — rather than the plain-text-with-markup view we have today.
For a demonstration of what current rendering looks like versus what rich rendering would produce, see Example: Current vs. Rich Rendering.
Implementation routes:

html:ul.html:li: Embed the forester dev server output directly. We already serve the rendered forest at http://localhost:1313. An embedded browser (EAF / xwidget-webkit) could visit the URL for the current tree. This is the cheapest path: no new rendering code, and every Forester feature (math, Datalog, transclusions, themes) works out of the box.

Parse tree + render to a rich Emacs buffer. Convert Forester markup to overlays, images (for math), and text properties in a native buffer. Keeps everything Emacs-native but requires reimplementing a nontrivial fraction of the compiler.
Hybrid. Use native buffer for editing, embedded browser in a side window for preview. Auto-refresh on save.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Open questions:

html:ul.html:li: Does xwidget-webkit reliably handle KaTeX / MathJax? Forester uses KaTeX; if the embedded browser can't run it, math renders as raw source.
How do we round-trip clicks in the embedded rendering back to "open this tree in Emacs"? The existing [edit] button (see Open Editor) already goes the other way.
Server dependency: option 1 assumes a live ./server.sh. Fine on my laptop; less fine if I open a tree on a machine without the forester toolchain.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Referenced from Rich Forest Rendering in Emacs. Shows concrete examples of Forester markup that renders well in a browser but degrades to plain text in the current Emacs preview.
Inline math. Source: #{e^{i \pi} + 1 = 0}. In-browser: e^{i \pi } + 1 = 0. In current Emacs preview: the raw source, with no KaTeX rendering.
Display math. Source: ##{\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n!} = e}. In-browser:
In the current Emacs preview this shows up as one long line of TeX-looking source with no formatting.
Inline markup. \em{italic}, \strong{bold}, and \code{monospace} all have visual distinction in the browser but currently flatten to indistinguishable runs of characters in the text preview.

Transclusion. A \transclude{sss-XXXX} call in the browser expands the target tree inline, often with its own math, code, and links. In the Emacs preview it shows as a literal \transclude call — the reader has to navigate away to see the content.

Datalog queries. Source like the status-pending query in Features for Forking Forester produces a live list of trees in the browser but renders as a raw \query\datalog{...} block in Emacs with no results.
Links and cross-references. [title](sss-XXXX) is a clickable navigation in the browser; in the Emacs preview it's plain text with no indication that it's a link target.

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Modern Web Browser from Within Emacs

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Investigate embedding a modern web browser (full HTML/CSS/JS, not just eww) inside Emacs. Candidates include emacs-application-framework (EAF), xwidget-webkit, and similar WebKit-based options.
Motivations:

html:ul.html:li: Stay in Emacs. Browsing the web without leaving the editor keeps keybindings, buffer management, and workflow consistent.

Lean proof widgets. Running a real React-capable renderer inside Emacs would let lean-mode display the interactive proof widgets that are currently Lean-exclusive to VSCode. See Lean Proof Widgets in Emacs.

Rich forest rendering. Replace the plain-text tree preview with a proper rendering of the compiled Forester HTML (math, transclusions, layouts, Datalog query results). See Rich Forest Rendering in Emacs.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Open questions:

html:ul.html:li: EAF vs. xwidget-webkit: which is more maintainable on macOS? EAF requires a Python backend and a compatible Qt/WebEngine; xwidget-webkit needs Emacs built with the --with-xwidgets flag, which is not default in Homebrew builds.
How much of this can be done with a headless render + image display instead of a live embedded browser? For static forest previews that may be enough; proof widgets need a live JS runtime.
Security posture: an embedded browser running arbitrary JS inside Emacs has a bigger blast radius than a normal editor. Should it be sandboxed or scoped to local URLs only?
